full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to issuance of this Rule may be summarised which are as follows: The First and Second Opposite Parties as plaintiffs instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 32 of 1980 in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge at Comilla for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the suit land. The suit on transfer to the court of the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 172 of 1981. Case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that Chandra Mohan Chowdhury was the owner of the suit land comprising of an area of 0.01 acre of land situated at Mohamaya Bazar. Chandra Mohan Chowdhury settled the same with structures standing thereon in favour of Abdul Jalil Mizi, defendant No. 8 who executed and registered a kabuliyat dated 23-8-1951 on his behalf as well as his full-brother Abdul Jabbar Mizi, the predecessor of defendant Nos.  1 and 2 Abdul Jalil Mizi, acquired the suit land out of the joint family fund for his own benefits and also for the benefit of his full-brother Abdul Jabbar. On amicable partition Abdul Jabbar Mizi used to own and possess northern half of the suit land with the structure described in schedule 1(ka) to the plaint and Abdul Jalil Mizi, used to own and possess the remaining southern portion of the land with the structure described in schedule 1(kah) to the plaint. During Revisional Settlement Operation the suit land was recorded both in the names of Abdul Jalil Mizi and Abdul Jabbar Mizi in Revisional Settlement Khatian No. 134 in equal shares. Abdul Jabbar Mizi transferred his portion of land with structure standing thereon to Serajul Islam Mizi, the defendant No. 9 by registered sale deed dated 16-9-1970 and possession was handed over to the transferee Serajul Islam Mizi. During the War of Liberation Abdul Jabbar Mizi died leaving behind two sons defendant Nos.   1 and 2 who approached their cousin defendant No. 9 in the year 1972 to permit them to start tea stall in ''Ka'' schedule land and permission was accordingly accorded by the defendant No. 9 and the defendant Nos.   1 and 2 since then remained there as licensees under defendant No. 9. Abdul Jalil Mizi also transferred his portion of land with structures thereon in favour of defendant No. 9 by a registered deed of conveyance dated 1-2-1977 and parted with possession. Defendant No. 9 allowed his uncle defendant No. 4 to run a business in the southern half of schedule ''Ka'' land as a licensee. The defendant Nos.   5 and 6 are the sons of defendant No. 4. The defendant No. 9 being the absolute owner over the suit land and the structures standing thereon, transferred the same in favour of the plaintiffs by way of two registered sale deeds dated 23-6-1979. The plaintiff, after purchase asked the defendant Nos.1-6 to hand over the vacant possession of the suit property in his favour. The defendants got no right, title and interest in the suit land. They having declined to give vacant possession of the suit property, the plaintiffs have been constrained to institute the suit for the reliefs stated above. 

 3. The defendant Nos.   1 and 2 contested the suit by presenting joint written statement which was thereafter supplemented by Better Statement. In the written statement it is stated that the suit land was self acquired property of Abdul Jalil Mizi, defendant No. 8 and while in possession allowed his full-brother Abdul Jabbar Mizi to start business on the northern half of the suit land. Abdul Jabbar Mizi having fallen in great financial distress, with the permission of Abdul jalil Mizi, transferred the schedule 1 (ka, land with structure thereon in favour of Serajul Islam Mizi, defendant No. 9 by registered sale deed dated 16-9-1970 and the said sale deed was accompanied with a contemporaneous registered deed of agreement for reconveyance. During the War of Liberation of the year 1971, the structure on the suit land was set on fire by Pakistan Occupation Army and Abdul Jabbar Mizi was also killed by the Army. It is also averred that defendant No. 8 made an oral gift with respect to schedule 1(ka) land in the middle part of the year 1972 and defendant Nos. 1 and 2 after reconstruction of the but started a Tea Stall. It is also pleaded that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 let out a portion of their but to defendant No. 3, Kalu Patwary as a monthly tenant on 18-7-1979. It is again asserted that the defendant No. 8 in confirmation of the earlier oral gift registered a deed of gift in favour of defendant Nos.   1 and 2 and the defendant No. 9 purchased the northern half of the suit land subject to an agreement of reconveyance and the land of schedule 1(ka) by operation of law stood redeemed in the year 1977 being the said deed a usufructuary mortgage. 

 4. The defendant No. 6 also filed a written statement taking the stand that the defendant No. 9 acquired no title on the basis of a purchase from Abdul Jabbar Mizi and Abdul Jalil Mizi. The further plea is that, the plaintiff acquired no legal right on the suit land on the basis of purchase from defendant No. 9 and their kabalas are illegal and void.'' 

 8. The defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 6, against the said decisions of the trial Judge, carried an appeal to the court of District Judge, Chandpur but without any success. The learned District Judge concurred with the decisions arrived at by the trial Judge who in agreement with the decisions of the trial Judge held that the story of oral gift is absolutely false and the plaintiffs acquired valid title on the suit land by purchase from defendant No. 9 in the year 1979 on the basis of two sale deeds. The learned District Judge also found that the deed of gift in favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is a collusive document created by defendant No. 8 who ceased to have any subsisting interest on the suit land long before the execution of the deed. The learned District Judge also recorded the finding that the plaintiffs instituted the suit within 12 years from 1972 when the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 first went into possession admittedly as licensees and entitled to the reliefs sought for subject to the right of redemption of schedule 1(ka) land by the legal heirs of late Abdul Jabbar according to law laid down in section 95(4) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Judge, thus, dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decrees passed by the trial Judge subject to the modification that the plaintiffs'' title to the disputed 1(ka) schedule land be declared subject to the right of redemption by the legal heirs of late Abdul Jabbar Mizi. 

 10. The plaintiff-opposite-parties appeared and opposed the Rule by filing an Affidavit-in-opposition. In the Affidavit-in-opposition it is stated that the Redemption Case No. 3 of 1987 filed by the defendant-petitioners has been allowed by the Upazila Revenue Officer on 8-6-1987 and on appeal preferred by the plaintiff-opposite-parties, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) being the appellate Authority allowed the said appeal. The order allowing the Redemption Case by the Upazila Revenue Officer and the order allowing the appeal on setting aside the order of redemption passed by the Upazila Revenue Officer are annexed in the Affidavit-in-opposition as Annexures-1 and 2 respectively. 

 13. The contention so raised is no doubt a question of law. But it is to be remembered that question of law follows from the fact proved. The defendants did neither set up this plea/contention in their written statement nor in the Memorandum of Appeal presented before the appellate Court nor taken as a ground in the Revisional application. This contention for the first time has been pressed into service before this Court orally at the time of the hearing of this Rule. This plea/contention, if would have been raised in the written statement or in the Memorandum of Appeal before the appellate Court, the plaintiff-opposite-parties would have got an opportunity to meet or to resist the same. The plaintiff-opposite-parties could not get any opportunity to meet and resist this plea. This plea having been for the first time raised orally before this Court at the time of hearing of the Rule, in exercising discretionary power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it is difficult for me to take into consideration of the said contention. The authorities cited from the side of the petitioners having been quite distinguishable in the facts and circumstances of the present case, the petitioners cannot get any benefit from those authorities. It is to be borne in mind that each and every judgment is to be made applicable in the facts and circumstance of each and every case and there cannot be any general application of the principles of law enunciated in any decision. 

 14. Let me now turn to a legal aspect of the matter which is a substantial question of law and is of a great public importance. The question is the redemption of the schedule 1 (ka) property by the legal heirs of Abdul Jabbar Mizi, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The learned District Judge came to the decision that the plaintiffs title to the schedule 1(Ka) land is liable to be declared subject to the right of redemption by the legal heirs of Abdul Jabbar Mizi. Admittedly, the sale deed dated 16-9-70 was accompanied by a contemporaneous agreement of reconveyance executed by the transferee Serajul Islam, defendant No. 9 in favour of Abdul Jabbar, the predecessor-father of defendant Nos. 1 and 2. In the said agreement of reconveyance it is stated that in the event of payment of consideration money fixed in the deed of sale within the period of 5 years from 1377 BS to month of Poush 1382 BS the transferee would be bound to deliver the possession of the said property to the transferor Abdul Jabbar Mizi. The certified copy of the agreement of reconveyance has been exhibited as Exhibit-C for the defendants. It appears from Annexure-1 annexed in the Affidavit-in-opposition filed by the plaintiff-opposite-parties that after the pronouncement of the judgment by the appellate Court, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by filing a Redemption Case got an order of redemption from the Upazila Nirbahi Officer. From Annexure-2 it further transpires that the said order of redemption passed by the Upazila Revenue Officer stood set aside on an appeal being Redemption Appeal No. 1 of 1987-88 preferred by the plaintiff-opposite-parties before the Additional. Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Chandpur who was the appellate authority. 

 15. It, thus, appears that the defendant Nos. 1 and .2 being encouraged with the decision of the learned District Judge approached the Upazila Revenue Officer to get the schedule 1 (Ka) property redeemed on the strength of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act though no attempt was ever made by the defendant Nos.   1 and 2 to get the land redeemed earlier possibly they being in possession of the Schedule 1(Ka) property. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) in his order dated 15-8-88 observed that since the matter in dispute remains pending before the High Court Division in Civil Revision Case, the decision of the High Court Division would be final. 

 16. Now the question comes whether the schedule 1(ka) property is liable to be redeemed under the purview of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 17. For the purpose of answering to the said question relevant provisions of law of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as SA Act), The Transfer of Property Act (hereinafter referred to TP Act) and Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to NAT Act) may profitably be noticed. 

 18. Under section 95A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act a transfer of a holding or of portion or share thereof either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferees any consideration or the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of, such holding or portion or share thereof for specified period in lieu of such consideration is deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 years and the provision of section 95 had been made applicable to such transfer whether made before or after the date of commencement of the Act (Second Amendment) Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 88 of 1972). 

 19. Section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides that a Raiyat could not enter into any form of usufructuary mortgage other than the complete usufructuary mortgage as defined in section 2 (6) of the Act and every such complete usufructuary mortgage is subject to the limitation of section 90 of the Act and the period for which such complete usufructuary mortgage may be entered by a Raiyat shall not exceed seven years. 

 23. A reading of section 95 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act manifests that a usufructuary mortgage can be effected in respect of a holding or a portion or share of the said holding. Holding is defined in section 2 (13) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is as follows : 

 "2(13). Holding means a parcel or parcels of land or an undivided share thereof, held by a raiyat or an under raiyat and forming the subject of a separate tenancy".

 28. "Non-agricultural land" is defined in section 2(4) of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 which is as follows : 

 (a) a homestead to which the provisions of section 182 of the Bengal Tenancy Act (VIII of 1885) apply, 

 30. "Non-agricultural Tenant" is defined in section 2(5) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act which is extracted hereunder : 

 32. "Bazar" is defined in section 2(12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is extracted hereunder : 

 33. In P Remanatha Aiyar's "The Law Lexicon" Bazar is stated as a market, a daily market, a market place. To constitute a Bazar all that is necessary is a place where buyers and sellers congregate to sell and buy. 

 35. Exhibit-5 is the Deed of Settlement dated 23-8-1951 executed and registered by the original owner Chandra Mohan Chowdhury in favour of Abdul Jalil. The schedule-1 property has been described as Chandina Bhiti (চান্দিনা ভিটি) and in the said deed the schedule 1(ka) property is stated to be situated at Mohamaya Bazar. 

 36. Exhibit-3 is the Deed of Conveyance dated 16-9-1970 executed by Abdul Jabbar Mizi in favour of Md. Serajul Islam the defendant No. 9. In the said deed the schedule 1(ka) property is stated as ChandinaBhiti land and the house standing thereon and the same is also stated to be situated at Mohamaya Bazar. Exhibit-C is the agreement of re-conveyance dated 16-9-70 executed by Serajul Islam in favour of Abdul Jabbar Mizi. In the said agreement of reconveyance also the schedule-1(ka) property has been described as Chandina Bhiti and is stated to be situated at Mohamaya Bazar. Exhibit-8(a) is the certified copy of the Record of Right of the relevant khatian No. 134 wherein the tenancy is stated to be a Non-agricultural tenancy right (সেকস্তি প্রজা স্বত্ব) and the schedule-1(ka) property has been stated to be shop (দোকান). 

 37. Having regard to the above provisions of law as well as the definitions it is evidently clear that schedule-1(ka) property is a Chandina  Bhiti and the same is situated at Mohamaya Bazar under Lodhergaon Mouza, Police Station-Chandpur and the said property is not an agricultural land. The schedule-1(ka) property is not held or possessed by a Raiyat and the same property is neither cultivatable nor covered with water at any time of the year. The suit property is shop (Dokan) situated at Mohamaya Bazar where people assemble there for the purpose of buying and selling agriculture or horticulture produces, articles of foods and other necessaries of life. The schedule 1(ka) property is, thus, an out and out a non-agricultural property is a non agricultural tenancy right. 

 38. Section 95A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is attracted only when a transfer of a holding or of portion of share thereof of an agricultural land either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey takes place and since the schedule-1(ka) property is not an agricultural land and the same being a non-agricultural property, the agreement of reconveyance dated 16-9-70 cannot be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage and the same cannot also stand redeemed tinder section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It is worthwhile to mention here that the Deed of Transfer and the agreement of reconveyance were executed on 16-9-70 before the amended section 95A of the said Act effected by President's Order 88 of 1972 and President''s Order 24 of 1973 came into force. President''s Order 88 of 1972 came into force on 3rd of August, 1972. 

 39. True it is that the deed of conveyance dated 16-9-70 having been accompanied with an agreement of reconveyance, by operation of law, on the strength of section 95A of the said Act, the said agreement of reconveyance can be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 years Provided the land is an agricultural land held by a raiyat and after the expiry of the said period of 7 years, the land in the Agreement of Reconveyarice can stand re-deemed. It has already been pointed out that since the redemption of the schedule 1(ka) Property does not come within the mischief of section 95A of the said Act, the question of redemption of the said property does not at all arise. The agreement of reconveyance having been contrary to law, the right or redemption cannot be enforced by invoking the provision of section 95A of the Act and the plaintiff-petitioners are not at all entitled to get the schedule-1(ka) property redeemed on the strength of the said section 95A of the Act. The title of the plaintiffs to schedule-1(ka) property is liable to be declared absolutely without any embargo and the decision of the learned District Judge to the effect that the plaintiffs'' title to the 1 (ka) schedule property is liable to be declared subject to the right of redemption by the legal heirs of late Abdul Jabbar Mizi stands set aside. The right of the plaintiffs to the schedule-1(ka) property is declared absolutely. The judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge is maintained with the modification stated above. 

 40. In view of the discussion made hereinbefore and the reasons stated I am of the considered view that the Rule is devoid of any substance and the same must be discharged.
